lines.text: You finished tuning by driving a square back onto the tape. Now the robot drives with nobody on the sticks, in the same kind of class you wrote once already for the arm and flywheel.
Don't expect accuracy from this one. A timer is enough to prove the pieces talk to each other, and that's the only job it has today.
Forward here means the robot's own forward, not the field's. Whichever way the front bumper points on the tape mark is the way it leaves.
The command itself is three steps: start driving, wait, send a stop. A wait is the only finish line you've got, because nothing on the drivetrain can say it has arrived.
A cancel skips whatever was left, and that includes the stop. So the canceled branch sends the same zero, and the wheels never depend on hands staying off the sticks.
The class around it stays thin. One method schedules the routine on enable. The other cancels it whenever the mode stops, and a disable counts.
Nothing in this routine tells the robot where it is on the field. Restart the robot code before a run you plan to measure, so the pose starts near zero and the distance is easy to read.
Set the room up before you enable. One person watches the robot, one keeps a thumb near disable, and enabling comes last.
Then four passes, in order. It runs on blocks first and on the floor once, and each pass answers a single question before you move on.
The third pass is the one that counts. Tape the floor before and after every run, and check the tape against the pose the robot logged.
Last, disable it about a second in. The wheels should stop, and when you enable again the routine starts over from its first line.
Write down three numbers: the taped distance, the end pose, and the wait that produced them. Next you'll draw a path from that same tape mark, and those numbers are what it has to match.
